title: Plans for God's Traveling Tent
overview: God asks Israel for freely given gifts and gives Moses detailed plans for a portable sanctuary and its most sacred furniture, so that he can live among them.

parts.label: Gifts given freely (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: The LORD asks for gifts only from people who want to give, so this is not a tax. The list covers what the tent and the priests' clothing would need, including stones for the high priest's special vest and chest piece, and the goods likely came from what Israel carried out of Egypt.

parts.label: A home among them (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: Here is the point of it all: God wants to live among his people, in a tent that can travel with them, built to a design he shows Moses. Christians later read this in light of Jesus, whom John's Gospel describes as God making his dwelling, literally pitching his tent, among people.

parts.label: The ark (vv. 10-16)
parts.note: The ark is a wooden chest covered in gold, roughly 1.1 meters long and 0.7 meters wide and high, made to hold the stone tablets of God's law. Its carrying poles stay in place permanently, so it is always ready to move with the people.

parts.label: The cover and cherubim (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: The solid gold lid's name is tied to the Hebrew idea of covering wrongs, and later blood was sprinkled on it on the yearly Day of Atonement, the day set aside for making amends for the people's wrongs (Leviticus 16). Between two winged figures called cherubim, whose exact look no one knows, the LORD promises to meet and speak with Moses, which many scholars compare to ancient kings seated on thrones guarded by winged creatures.

parts.label: The table and bread (vv. 23-30)
parts.note: A gold covered table holds dishes, pitchers for poured offerings, and the bread of the Presence, kept before the LORD at all times. Leviticus 24 later describes twelve loaves replaced every week, and many readers take the twelve as standing for Israel's twelve tribes, though the text does not spell that out.

parts.label: The lampstand (vv. 31-40)
parts.note: Hammered from pure gold in the shape of a flowering almond tree, the seven branched lampstand and all its tools together used one talent of gold, roughly 30 to 35 kilograms. Its lamps lit the holy room, some scholars see tree of life imagery in it, and the chapter ends by insisting again that everything follow the pattern shown on the mountain.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the tabernacle's many details were meant to picture Christ point by point, or mainly to show how Israel was to live with a holy God present among them, with only the broad themes pointing forward.
think: Why do you think people in so many cultures have wanted a special place set apart for meeting the divine, and has any place ever felt that way to you?
